newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Online giants accused of copyright scaremongering.
newsitem.headline: Online giants accused of copyright scaremongering.

text.p: The music industry, raising the heat in the battle to protect copyrights in cyberspace at Geneva negotiations, accused Internet giants on Monday of scaremongering to protect their multi-billion-dollar interests.

Online chiefs say controversial global pacts to revise copyright laws for the digital era expose them to multi-billion-dollar liability and give broad powers to music and other copyright-based businesses.

But Nicholas Garnett, head of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry lobby group whose 1,100 members include record producers BMG, EMI, MCA, Sony Music and PolyGram, accused online firms of "turning the truth on its head."
He said online firms had nothing to fear from the treaties.

"We are accusing them (online companies) of scaremongering. They're confusing the issue," he told a briefing. "They're promoting their own agenda to devalue the rights of copyright industries so they can set up services without having to pay."

Added Alan Dixon, a representative of the software industry: "Nobody held phone companies liable for information going through fax machines. Nobody is saying that telephone companies should be liable for things they have no knowledge of."

The presidents of 11 U.S. service giants including America Online, BellSouth Corporation and CompuServe wrote to U.S. President Bill Clinton last week, urging him to reconsider Washington's strong support for the draft treaties.
They say the treaties make even innocent Web-surfing, which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies, a violation of copyright rules.
U.S. assistant secretary of commerce, Bruce Lehman, has responded by saying the treaties did not limit fair use.
In Geneva, copyright industries are trying to ensure they get a cut from works on the Internet, the new medium for the distribution of literature, music, software and commerce.
The $40 billion-a-year music industry says electronic delivery of music recordings, negligible at present, could represent a $2 billion market in the coming years.

The conference, under United Nations auspices, has until December 20 to finalise discussions on three treaties on literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases.
